proposal: The Mandate calls for a final accounting and accelerated cleanup of fraud in the COVID-19 PPP and EIDL programs: consider bringing in private-sector help to close out the programs, require PPP borrowers that were not eligible for forgiveness to repay, refer borrowers who falsified applications to law enforcement, and cooperate with congressional oversight. It also asks SBA to determine whether it can reverse forgiveness for certain Planned Parenthood affiliates' PPP loans, which the chapter says exceeded the size limit, and to refer any knowing misstatements to the Justice Department.

status_summary: SBA's fraud enforcement has been large and operative in 2026, according to SBA's own releases. It began suspending borrowers by state (California, 2026-02-06), referred over 560,000 suspected fraudulent borrowers tied to about $22 billion to Treasury for collection (2026-04-24), and on 2026-09-14 announced suspensions of 870,000 borrowers tied to about $39 billion in suspected fraud, final demand letters, and DOJ results (more than 160 criminal defendants, about $245 million in intended loss). On 2026-09-23 SBA said an IRS comparison of loan applications and tax records found discrepancies tied to about $100 billion in loans and that IRS examinations had opened. The releases do not report total funds recovered. No action on the Planned Parenthood PPP loans or on reversing forgiveness for ineligible PPP loans was found, and no private-sector close-out contractor was identified.

timeline.event: SBA Office of Inspector General issues report 25-12 on SBA's actions regarding forgiven PPP loans later flagged as potentially ineligible; further 2025 reports address EIDL collection and servicing (25-23, 25-16) and PPP loans over size standards (25-14).
SBA suspends about 111,600 California borrowers tied to roughly $8.6 billion in suspected fraudulent PPP and EIDL activity; later state actions follow (Ohio 2026-06-04, Wisconsin 2026-07-08).
SBA refers over 560,000 suspected fraudulent borrowers tied to about $22 billion in loans to Treasury for collection.

SBA OIG announced a partnership with the Department of Justice to launch the National Fraud Detection Center, a prosecutor-led effort to coordinate federal and state fraud work; SBA OIG assigned analysts and investigators as a charter signatory.

SBA and IRS announced that an IRS comparison of loan application tax information with IRS records found discrepancies tied to about $100 billion in loans, from a referral of over $200 billion in suspected fraud earlier in 2026; IRS opened examinations. SBA states that individual cases will be judged on their facts and that no recovered amount is reported.

title: Complete COVID-era PPP and EIDL fraud cleanup, with repayment or referral
uncertainties: Suspected fraud figures come from SBA and SBA OIG releases (legacy.sba.gov pages opened on 2026-10-18) and from independent coverage cited in the red-team check; they describe suspected fraud, not adjudicated losses. Recoveries are reported by SBA OIG: an OIG release of 2026-04-07 (legacy.sba.gov) reports over 86.7 million dollars in direct returns coordinated by OIG to date and more than 2.8 billion dollars in total investigative recoveries involving suspected fraud in the COVID-19 relief programs, and the OIG Spring 2026 Semiannual Report to Congress (oversight.gov, covering 2025-10-01 to 2026-03-31) reports 83 indictments, 52 convictions and about 244.6 million dollars in investigative dollar accomplishments for the period, with a pandemic-program row of 63 investigations, 79 indictments, 56 arrests and 47 convictions. The 2.8 billion dollar figure is cumulative and not limited to actions since 2025-01-20, and investigative dollar accomplishments may include amounts ordered or agreed rather than collected (inference; the report's definition was not checked), so neither figure measures funds recovered under the 2026 enforcement actions. The OIG's 244.6 million dollars and the DOJ figure of about 245 million dollars in intended loss in the 2026-09-14 release are different measures and are not the same amount. The semiannual report lists an open recommendation (25-14-1) that SBA seek repayment of forgiveness amounts on ineligible loans, so reversal of forgiveness is an OIG recommendation, not a reported SBA action; the report's text extraction ended in Appendix F, so Appendix G was not read. The 2026-02-06 California suspension and 2026-04-24 Treasury referral dates come from the dated SBA releases linked in the 2026-09-14 release, whose own text describes those actions only as earlier ones. Earlier suspension rounds (Minnesota, Maine) lack dates in the sources. OIG report 25-12 (effective 2025-04-23; 37,938 forgiven PPP loans, about 4.6 billion dollars, with open clawback hold codes; management agreed to complete reviews and formalize recovery criteria) was read on its SBA page; it bears on recovering payments on ineligible forgiven loans but does not describe reversal of forgiveness by SBA, and it does not mention Planned Parenthood. No action was found, and none was exhaustively searched for, on the Planned Parenthood loans. The stage reflects the scale and operative status of enforcement.
